title: Private Deployments: Customer Requirements, Reference Architectures, and Day-2 Ops
author: Jordan Kim
body:
Purpose
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical guidance for private deployments (VPC and on-prem), covering: the customer requirements library, validated reference architectures, packaging and installation guidance for on-prem bundles, and operational (day-2) runbooks including upgrade and rollback procedures. Use this as the primary handoff artifact for Solutions, SRE, and Customer Engineering during onboarding and major lifecycle events.

Scope
- VPC-hosted private control plane and data plane deployments
- Air-gapped / on-prem appliance packaging and install
- Post-install day-2 operations: backup, monitoring, scaling, incident response
- Upgrade and rollback playbooks for minor and major releases
- Customer prerequisites checklist and acceptance criteria

Owners and contacts
- Product Owner: Marco Reyes (product)
- Technical Owner: Jordan Kim (serving runtime)
- Support/Oncall: eng-private-deployments rotation (see team roster)
- Escalation: Customer Success -> Solutions Eng -> Eng SRE (page: escalation-playbook)

High-level deployment models
1) VPC-managed Private (recommended for most enterprise customers)
   - Control plane managed by Redwood (control traffic via secure peering / AWS PrivateLink)
   - Data plane runs in customer VPC (EKS / self-managed k8s or dedicated instances)
   - Good fit when customer requires network isolation and customer-managed keys

2) Fully on-prem appliance (air-gapped)
   - All control and data plane components run inside customer network
   - Requires on-prem packaging (OCI images + deployment bundle, offline registry, and install shim)
   - Good fit for regulated workloads or customers with no outbound connectivity

3) Hybrid (control plane in Redwood region, data plane on customer hardware)
   - Tradeoff: simpler upgrades vs. stronger data residency control

Customer requirements library (checklist and acceptance criteria)
- Security and compliance
  - Customer must provide an approved KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or HSM) or agree to Redwood-managed KMS for VPC deployments.
  - RBAC expectations: SAML/SCIM or OIDC integration required for SSO (list supported providers).
  - Legal: Completed DPA and any required SOC2/ISO addenda.
- Network / Connectivity
  - CIDR ranges for peering and NAT: provide /24 allocation for control plane peering and /20 for data-plane autoscaling (examples included).
  - Required outbound endpoints (if not air-gapped): package registry endpoint, telemetry endpoints, time servers.
  - Ports: allow inbound ports 80/443 to the load balancer; internal ports 8000-8100 for runtime RPC between nodes (see config table).
- Compute & Storage
  - Minimum node types: GPU accelerated hosts (NVIDIA A10/A100 recommended) or multi-GPU MPS configurations for high throughput.
  - Minimum cluster size for production: 3 GPU nodes + 3 CPU control nodes for HA (detailed sizing matrix below).
  - Persistent storage: 1 TiB SSD per model serving node (for KV caches and model shard storage); backup target with >= 3x redundancy.
- Identity and secrets
  - Service account with least privilege for registry pulls and S3-compatible storage.
  - KMS key ARNs for encryption-at-rest.
- Observability and logging
  - Customer must provide an endpoint for log ingestion (syslog / TLS) or allow Redwood managed ingestion.
  - Prometheus scrape permissions and Grafana access (if integrated into customer monitoring).

Minimal hardware and sizing matrix (example)
- Development / PoC:
  - 1 x GPU node (A10) + 1 control node, 128 GiB RAM, 1 TiB NVMe
- Small production:
  - 3 x GPU nodes (A10/A100 small), 6 x vCPUs per node, 256 GiB RAM, 3 TiB NVMe total
- Medium production:
  - 6-12 GPU nodes, 12-24 vCPUs per node, 512 GiB RAM, network-attached storage for model cache

Reference architecture patterns
- VPC Managed Private (multi-AZ)
  - Diagram (text): Customer VPC subnets -> PrivateLink endpoint to Redwood control plane -> Internal ALB -> EKS nodes hosting inference runtime -> EFS / S3 for model store -> KMS for key management
  - Failure domains: design for AZ isolation: at least two AZs for critical control and data plane services

- On-prem Air-gapped (appliance)
  - Local registry (Harbor) serving OCI images, offline artifacts bundle, bootstrap host with deployment shim, local monitoring stack (Prometheus + Grafana), and optional remote support tunnel established by customer for out-of-band support.

On-prem packaging and install guide (high-level)
1) Preparation
   - Validate hardware, network, and storage against the customer requirements checklist.
   - Provision an internal registry and upload Redwood OCI images or provide offline bundle via secure file transfer.
2) Bootstrap host
   - One bootstrap host with internet or secure file transfer to load the offline bundle.
   - Run install.sh --bundle <path> --mode airgap --kubeconfig <kubeconfig>
3) Registry and images
   - Configure internal registry credentials and mirror images: mirror.yaml example provided below.
4) Deploy control plane components and CRDs (namespace redwood-system)
   - kubectl apply -f redwood-controlplane.yaml
5) Post-install validation (see Day-2 validation checklist)

Sample mirror.yaml (example)
# mirror configuration for internal registry
- images: ["registry.redwood.ai/runtime:2026.01", "registry.redwood.ai/controlplane:2026.01"]
  destination: harbor.local/redwood
  auth: "/etc/harbor/credentials.json"

Day-2 operations (runbooks and playbooks)
- Health checks and periodic tasks
  - Daily: verify node readiness, runtime process health, and model cache hit rates.
  - Weekly: rotate logs and validate backup job completion.
  - Monthly: capacity planning review and simulated failover test.
- Common runbooks
  - Model serving degraded latency: check GPU utilization, KV cache hit-rate, batch sizes, and tail latency SLOs. If GPU saturation, scale GPU pool or apply adaptive batching config.
  - Control plane unavailability: failover to secondary control plane region (if configured) or rollback to previous stable chart (see rollback playbook).

Backup and restore
- Backup scope: Kubernetes control plane manifests (Helm releases), PV snapshots, model store snapshots, Redis/KV backups, and metadata DB (Postgres) dumps.
- Recovery objectives: RPO <= 30 minutes for metadata DB (when configured with WAL shipping), RTO <= 2 hours for model-serving nodes (assuming cold restore from object store).
- Example PV snapshot command (CSI snapshot):
  kubectl create -f snapshot-class.yaml
  kubectl create -f snapshot-claim.yaml

Upgrade and rollback procedures
- Upgrade types
  - Patch (minor) upgrade: rolling update of runtime pods and control-plane deployments; safe to run during business hours with canary traffic.
  - Minor version upgrade: similar but with additional DB migrations that are reversible via migration scripts.
  - Major upgrade: may include incompatible model cache format changes; recommended maintenance window and full backup before starting.

- Pre-upgrade checklist (must be verified before upgrade)
  1) Completed full backups for database, model-store, and PVs.
  2) Health: 100% control plane readiness, 95% node readiness.
  3) Open critical incidents: none.
  4) Scheduled maintenance window communicated to stakeholders.
  5) Canary targets configured (10% traffic routed to canary).

- Rolling upgrade procedure (example for minor release)
  1) Tag release image and upload to registry.
  2) Deploy canary: update deployment redwood-runtime-canary with new image.
  3) Monitor canary for 30 minutes: latency, error-rate, memory/GPU metrics.
  4) If canary looks healthy, begin 10% -> 50% -> 100% rollout in 15-30 minute increments.
  5) If at any step SLI thresholds breached, run rollback steps immediately.

- Rollback playbook (fast rollback)
  1) Pause rollout and scale canary to 0.
  2) Re-deploy previous stable image to affected deployments: kubectl set image deployment/redwood-runtime <container>=registry.redwood.ai/runtime:stable
  3) Validate traffic shifts back to stable and monitor SLOs for 30 minutes.
  4) Open a postmortem and capture traces/logs for triage.

DB migration guidance
- Use idempotent migrations where possible. For irreversible migrations, use a two-phase approach: write-path enablement followed by background conversion, then read-path flip once conversion reaches 100%.

Observability and SLOs (examples)
- Latency SLO: P95 <= 200ms for local conversational workloads, P99 <= 1.5s (adjust per model family).
- Error budget policy: team SLO and burn rate thresholds are in eng-sre/runbooks.
- Key dashboards: per-route latency, token-level cost, GPU utilization, cache hit-rate, and model shard distribution.

Security and compliance controls
- Audit logging: all admin actions recorded to customer-managed SIEM when required.
- Secrets: use KMS for root keys; limit plaintext secret access to bootstrap host only.
- Vulnerability management: apply CVE patching schedule quarterly and patch critical CVEs within 72 hours.

Acceptance & handoff checklist (pre-go-live)
- All items in the customer requirements library validated and signed off by customer security lead.
- Production smoke tests: generation throughput, latency SLO validation, and model correctness checks passed.
- Backup restore test executed end-to-end using a point-in-time snapshot.
- Operations runbook handed off to customer oncall and Redwood support team with runbook readout session.

Appendices
A) Common k8s manifests and Helm values (examples)
- redwood-values.yaml: contains resource limits, image tags, network config, and KMS integration examples.
B) Troubleshooting quick commands
- kubectl top pods -n redwood
- kubectl logs -l app=redwood-runtime -n redwood --tail 200
C) Contact matrix and escalation flow
- When to contact Redwood Support vs. Eng SRE vs. Product: provided with phone and pager rotation details (internal).

Notes
This document is intended to be a living reference. For customer-specific deviations (special compliance requirements, bespoke networking architectures), create a child page under confluence eng-private-deployments/<customer-name> and link back to this canonical page. For any proposed changes to core procedures, open an ADR in architecture-and-standards.
